'''Slayton A. Evans Jr.''' (May 17, 1943 – March 24, 2001) was an American chemist and professor at the [[University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill]]. He was a leading researcher into organophosphorus chemistry. His research led to a greater understanding of the functions of [[organophosphate]] compounds and innovations in methods to produce chemical compounds for pharmaceutical drugs.

==Early life and education==
Slayton Alvin Evans Jr. was born on May 17, 1943, in Chicago, Illinois, to Corine M. Thompson Evans and Slayton A. Evans, Sr.<ref name="AASMI">{{cite book |last1=Spangenburg |first1=Ray |last2=Moser |first2=Diane |last3=Long |first3=Douglas |title=African Americans in Science, Math, and Invention |date=2014 |publisher=Infobase Publishing |isbn=978-1-4381-0774-5 |pages=74–75 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XSOZ8kF5ynEC&pg=PA74 |language=en |chapter=Evans, Slayton Alvin Jr.}}</ref><ref name="ABC-CLIO"/> Months later, his father was called to serve in [[World War II]].<ref name="DAAS"/> When Slayton was three years old, the family moved to [[Meridian, Mississippi]],<ref name="ABC-CLIO"/> where they lived in a segregated [[Subsidized housing in the United States|public housing project]] and his father worked at a [[J. C. Penney]] store. Slayton's interest in chemistry began early, when he was given a chemistry set. In addition, a small microscope allowed him to study various plant specimens and insects. Evans and his two younger siblings enrolled at a [[racial segregation|segregated]] primary school run by the [[Roman Catholic Church]], and later he attended St. Joseph's High School. In 1957, when Evans was in the ninth grade, news of the artificial satellite [[Sputnik 1|Sputnik]] inspired him to learn about rocketry and attempt to build his own. While he was given permission by the nuns at his school to buy chemicals to make [[rocket fuel]], he had to make his own powdered charcoal. He built six rockets, two of them achieving liftoff.<ref name="DAAS">{{cite book |last1=Kessler |first1=James H. |last2=Morin |first2=Katherine A. |last3=Kidd |first3=J. S. |last4=Kidd |first4=Renee A. |title=Distinguished African American Scientists of the 20th Century |date=1996 |publisher=Greenwood Publishing Group |isbn=978-0-89774-955-8 |pages=87–91 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-ydHVdMUqdEC&pg=PA87 |language=en |chapter=Slayton A. Evans Jr.}}</ref>

Evans helped pay for his school tuition by mowing lawns and during eighth grade he was a junior assistant janitor at his elementary school. Later he worked in the high school cafeteria. In his third year of high school, he considered going into the [[United States Air Force|Air Force]], but was too tall for flight training. However, he took several competitive examinations and was the recipient of an academic scholarship to [[Tougaloo College]] where he also received an athletic scholarship for basketball.  He enrolled at Tougaloo in 1961.<ref name="DAAS"/>

By the end of his first year, Evans had top marks in chemistry in his class. He got a summer job working for the pharmaceutical company [[Abbott Laboratories]] in Chicago where he was tasked first with creating chemical compounds from raw materials, and later with identifying the stages of chemical reactions.<ref name="DAAS"/> Evans graduated from Tougaloo with a Bachelor of Science in chemistry in 1965.<ref name="ABC-CLIO"/> Evans was encouraged to attend graduate school, though he didn't know how to pay for it. He briefly attended the [[Illinois Institute of Technology]] before transferring to [[Case Western Reserve University]] in Cleveland, Ohio, where he was offered a research assistant position in the chemistry department. In his first year, he received a draft notice to go to the [[Vietnam War]]. University officials contacted the draft board and explained that Evans' research was crucial to the war effort. He was researching a medicine to treat [[schistosomiasis]], a disease caused by parasitic flatworms that are common in Southeast Asia. He completed his coursework in 1969 and received his Ph.D. in chemistry in early 1970.<ref name="DAAS"/>

==Research and academic career==
Evans took a postdoctoral fellowship at the [[University of Texas at Arlington]] for the 1970–1971 academic year, followed by second fellowship at the [[University of Notre Dame]] in Indiana,<ref name="AASMI"/> where he worked with the organic chemist [[Ernest L. Eliel]] studying [[stereochemistry]].<ref name="DAAS"/> Upon the completion of the fellowship, he was invited to be a research instructor at [[Dartmouth College]] in 1972,<ref name="AASMI"/><ref name="ABC-CLIO"/> though they did not have the laboratory equipment he required to continue his research.<ref name="DAAS"/> Evans then joined the faculty of the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] as an assistant professor of chemistry in 1974.<ref name="AASMI"/><ref name="ABC-CLIO"/> He was the first African-American chemistry professor at the university.<ref name="CC">{{cite news |last1=Magaw |first1=Jim |title=Carolina's first African-American chemist honored with lecture fund |url=http://givingpubs.unc.edu/documents/carolina_connections/archives/fall2003/evans.html |work=Carolina Connections |date=2003 |access-date=June 19, 2020 |archive-date=June 21, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200621094446/http://givingpubs.unc.edu/documents/carolina_connections/archives/fall2003/evans.html |url-status=live }}</ref> After 10 years at Chapel Hill, Evans became a full professor, and in 1992 was honored with a Kenan Professor chair.<ref name="DAAS"/>

Evans was a leading researcher in the field of organophosphorus chemistry,<ref name="ABC-CLIO"/> authoring more than 85 scientific articles on organosulfur and organophosphorus chemistry.<ref name="AASMI"/> His research led to a deeper understanding of the functions of [[organophosphate]] compounds and innovations in methods to produce chemical compounds for pharmaceutical drugs. Evans was inspired by [[William Standish Knowles]], who in 1968 developed a method of [[asymmetric hydrogenation]], which Evans used to develop alternative [[asymmetric synthesis]] methods as a way to produce single [[stereoisomer]]s. Evans started experimenting with organophosphorus chemistry in 1970, developing a process using phosphorus atoms of organophosphate compounds as agents to produce specific stereoisomers. He also devised a method of asymmetric synthesis to synthesize alpha-amino phosphonic acids by adding phosphorus to [[sulfimide]]s.<ref name="ABC-CLIO">{{cite book |last1=Carey Jr. |first1=Charles W. |title=African Americans in Science: An Encyclopedia of People and Progress |date=2008 |publisher=ABC-CLIO |isbn=978-1-85109-999-3 |pages=75–76 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4rZzCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA75 |language=en |chapter=Evans, Slaton A. Jr.}}</ref>

At the [[University of North Carolina]] Evans assembled a research team of undergraduates, graduate students, and postdoctoral fellows from around the world. In the 1980s, a [[Ford Foundation Fellowship]] allowed him to create ties between his research team and a research group at the [[Paul Sabatier University]] in France, where he spent a full sabbatical year. Later, with the help of a [[Fulbright Fellowship]], he built ties with groups in Mexico, Poland, Germany, Greece, and Russia.<ref name="DAAS"/>

Evans championed recruiting minority applicants to UNC-Chapel Hill,<ref name="CC"/> while on the national front, he served on committees of the [[American Chemical Society]], the [[National Institutes of Health]], the [[National Science Foundation]], and was chair of the U.S. National Committee of the [[International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry]].<ref name="DAAS"/><ref name="ABC-CLIO"/><ref name="CC"/> He also served on a council that advised the [[National Institute of General Medical Sciences]].<ref name="ABC-CLIO"/>

==Awards and recognition==
*1994 — Tanner Award for Teaching Excellence<ref name="DAAS"/>
*1995 — NSF Special Creativity Award in Organophosphorus Chemistry
*1998 — ACS Award for Encouraging Disadvantaged Students into Careers in the Chemical Sciences
*Chancellor's Award for Excellence in Undergraduate Education
*Howard University Outstanding Achievement Award

==Personal life==
Evans married Tommie Johnson in 1967. They had two children. Evans died on March 24, 2001, in [[Chapel Hill, North Carolina|Chapel Hill]]. The Slayton A. Evans Jr. Memorial Lecture Fund<ref name="CC"/> and the Slayton Evans Research Award were both named in his honor post-humously.<ref name="ABC-CLIO"/>
